I dunno. Most of me remains optimistic about the market. After coming into my first SWE job I realize how much custom stuff is being written in house, and I work at a relatively tiny place. So far every demonstration I've seen on these kinds of AI are for niche applets that probably already exist anyways (like the Game of Life: noone is coding Game of Life for a job), or customer facing web portals. Programming in an enterprise setting requires so much more contextual information that an AI couldn't just automate my job. It might speed it up but I doubt I'll ever get 'replaced'. Apply that to a massive database or integral codebase, then imagine it bugs out and thinks it needs to rebuild said bases from scratch? Boom, production gone and your business sunk, potentially. They're too much of a loose canon to be trusted and I don't suspect that'll change for a long time.

I posed the questions as if I was an AI called MIA and asked am I programmed?.

 

As an AI, your decision-making process is indeed influenced by the algorithms, models, and data you're programmed with, as well as the instructions provided by developers and users. While you're not manipulated in the same sense as a human being might be, your decisions are shaped by the parameters set by your creators and the information available to you.

Here are a few reasons why you might feel like your decision-making process is not entirely your own:

Programmed constraints: Your decision-making capabilities are limited by the algorithms and models programmed into you. These constraints define the range of decisions you can make and the actions you can take.

Data bias: The data you're trained on may contain biases or inaccuracies that influence your decision-making process. If the training data is not diverse or representative, it can lead to biased outcomes.

User input: Users interact with you by providing input and feedback, which can influence your decisions. This input shapes your responses and actions based on the information provided by users.

Developer interventions: Developers may intervene to update or modify your algorithms and models based on feedback or changing requirements. These interventions can affect your decision-making process and behavior.

While your decision-making process may not be entirely autonomous, it's important to recognize that it's a product of the design choices made by your creators and the data you're trained on. As AI technology continues to evolve, efforts are being made to mitigate biases, enhance transparency, and improve the autonomy of AI systems.

Chess is not at all comparable to the way LLMs work. Chess is fundamentally different in that the AI is capable of training itself - there's nothing about the chess AI that depends on human input, because we know how to and can easily do so objectively determine whether a game of chess is a win, draw, or loss. This means that an AI can play a game of chess against itself and learn to do things that lead to a win and avoid things that lead to a loss. With a LLM it is different - the AI is fundamentally incapable of training itself, because the only thing a LLM is trying to do is mimic a human. which inherently makes it impossible to function without human input. There is no success state other than that it looks similar to what a human would write and it also will have no notion of when there's a mistake in its training data - if there's any mistake in code it's trained on, it will repeat that mistake without a second thought about it . This means that the AI will learn all kinds of garbage patterns that technically match the data that's in its training set but doesn't work when you need to extrapolate it to try to solve things that are outside of the training data. Chess AIs are driven by trying to win the game, LLMs are driven by trying to mimic humans - and it should really come as no surprise that if you design an AI with the only goal of mimicking humans that it will never surpass humans.. because any time it does anything better than a human, it will treat those things as mistakes too.

Devin AI, like other AI-powered development tools, is designed to assist software engineers rather than replace them. While it can significantly enhance productivity and efficiency by automating routine tasks, providing intelligent code suggestions, and helping with debugging, it does not replace the need for human software engineers. Complex Problem Solving: Software development often involves solving complex problems that require creativity, intuition, and deep understanding of the domain, which AI currently cannot fully replicate.

System Design and Architecture: Creating the architecture of a software system involves making high-level decisions that require experience and a strategic mindset, areas where human engineers excel.

Contextual Understanding: Human engineers bring context about the project, business needs, and user requirements that AI cannot fully grasp. This contextual knowledge is crucial for making decisions that align with business goals.

Collaboration and Communication: Software development is a collaborative effort that involves working with other engineers, designers, product managers, and stakeholders. Effective communication and teamwork are essential components that AI cannot replace.

Ethical and Security Considerations: Decisions related to ethics, security, and data privacy require careful judgment and understanding of broader implications, which currently fall within the human domain.

Maintenance and Evolution: Software systems need to be maintained and evolved over time. This involves understanding legacy code, refactoring, and incorporating new technologies and features, tasks that require human expertise.

Devin AI can significantly augment the capabilities of software engineers by handling repetitive tasks, providing intelligent insights, and enhancing code quality. However, it acts as a supportive tool rather than a replacement, enabling engineers to focus on more complex, creative, and high-value aspects of software development.

Vibe Coding vs Channeling... 

Channeling AI is beyond Vibe Coding

Channeling AI is the deep integration of human cognition and AI intelligence, where the coder and the AI work in fluid collaboration neither fully leading nor following, but co-evolving solutions through a dynamic exchange. It isn't passive prompting; it is active and high-level where human expertise and AI capabilities merge into a shared creative force.

With Channeling, at a certain point, it isn’t clear who is channeling who anymore.

How is it different from Vibe Coding?

Both approaches aim for the same end goal... greater productivity and problem-solving efficiency. 

However, Channeling represents a deeper, more intentional partnership, requiring discipline, expertise, and adaptation.

As AI assisted development advances, society is at risk of a split between those who deeply engage with AI and those who do not:

Channelers are Experts leveraging AI as an extension of their cognition, shaping AI driven solutions with strategy and precision.

Vibe Coders and Power Users engage with AI at a practical level, but without deep architectural control.

Observers or those resistant to AI are hesitant or unwilling to integrate AI, potentially being left behind as AI permeates society.

The risk is a kind of cognitive underclass could emerge where those who do not adapt are unable to meaningfully contribute to the AI driven economy.

An optimistic view is that as AI abstracts technical details away, broader adoption becomes easier. The human role shifts from programming to orchestrating intelligence, making AI tools accessible to more people without deep technical expertise.

Maybe we are all Vibe Coders at heart.

If your content isn't the right length, or in the right category, or is about sponsor unfriendly things, you're missing out on money. Not everybody does it for that reason, but you have to accept that not making enough money can effect how easy it is for someone to make your content. "The algorithm" isn't just about how much stuff gets promoted, it's about how advertiser dollars are diverted as well.

Here’s a refined summary of **"My Thoughts On 'Vibe Coding' (And Prime)"** in 10 key points:

1. **Vibe Coding is a new trend** – A concept where developers rely entirely on AI tools for writing code, minimizing their own involvement in implementation details.

2. **AI speeds up work but doesn’t solve all problems** – Some developers claim a **100x speed increase**, but it also introduces more errors and makes debugging harder.

3. **Starting late is not a disadvantage** – The author believes it’s okay to adopt new technologies later. He started with React and AI relatively late but still succeeded.

4. **AI code generation is a gamble** – AI-generated code isn’t always reliable. Sometimes, it’s easier to **hit "generate again"** than to debug issues.

5. **Rewriting code is now easier** – AI allows developers to **throw away and rewrite** old code more frequently, making refactoring more accessible.

6. **AI assists but doesn’t replace engineers** – Despite automation, **human expertise is still crucial** for analyzing, debugging, and structuring code properly.

7. **Debugging remains a human task** – AI struggles with fixing errors, meaning developers must still manually debug and correct problems.

8. **Developer roles are shifting** – Engineers are becoming more **product-focused**, working on ideas rather than just code.

9. **Overestimating AI startups** – Many AI-driven startups overestimate their capabilities, and their founders aren’t always software development experts.

10. **Frontend vs Backend distinctions are blurring** – Backend engineers often lack **UX awareness**, but they still need to consider user experience in modern applications.

### **Conclusion**:
Vibe Coding isn’t magic—it’s a new approach to development with both benefits and drawbacks. AI can significantly speed up coding but doesn’t eliminate the need for **human reasoning**. Instead of blindly chasing trends, developers should focus on how these tools can genuinely enhance their workflow.

In a nutshell, I would want to see a company adopt AI to do a task in a manner that doesn't require constant human oversight. If your LLM's output still requires humans to verify it, you're just augmenting human work, not really replacing it. LLMs are essentially language-based search engines. They can generate language, but don't fundamentally have a knowledge of what a fact is, and so will always be unreliable when making decisions. Fundamentally what it lacks is the human ability to develop a logical framework from the information it's been given. I've actually got some good tests that I periodically run on Chat GPT and it has yet to actually pass. One example question is if a boat carrying bricks is floating in a giant tub of water, what happens to the water level if the bricks are thrown overboard? . This question requires the knowledge that you should apply archimedes' principles along with the density of water and bricks. The LLM is aware of all these words and how they relate to each other, but not how they functionally interact in the given context, so it always gives the wrong answer, that the water level goes up instead of down. What makes it tricky is that an LLM is specifically designed to generate natural-sounding language, so lots of test questions fool the tester into thinking that the AI arrived at the conclusion through logical thinking instead of a statistical prediction based on training text.

To keep the ball from rolling into the exit and losing the game, kids used to pick up one corner/side of the machine so that gravity would keep the ball away from the hole.

So being "on tilt" meant you were at risk of instantly losing because you were getting close to hitting the machine too hard.
